items.title: Hastings lasted nearly a full day and was won by a feigned retreat
items.claim: The Battle of Hastings (14 October 1066) is often remembered as a swift Norman triumph. What actually happened?

options.text: William routed Harold's army within an hour
Fighting lasted from around 9 a.m. to dusk; the Anglo-Saxon shield-wall held until Norman cavalry used feigned retreats to draw housecarls down Senlac Hill, exposing the line
The English never engaged — they fled at the sight of Norman cavalry
The battle was decided by a single cavalry charge at dawn

items.reveal_title: A near thing on Senlac Hill
items.reveal:
William of Poitiers and the Bayeux Tapestry both record the day-long fight. Harold's army held the high ground in a shield-wall formation; William's archers, infantry and cavalry attacked uphill. A rumour that William had died spread early; he raised his helmet to show his face and rally his troops.

The feigned retreats — possibly accidental at first, then deliberate — broke the discipline of the shield-wall. Harold was killed late in the day along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine.

William was not crowned at Westminster until 25 December 1066. Anglo-Saxon resistance continued for years (the Harrying of the North, 1069-70).
items.why: 1066 looks decisive in retrospect. On the day it was a hill-defence that nearly held — and might have, if not for a tactical innovation. Contingency in military history.

items.title: Harold won the first battle of 1066 — then lost the second three weeks later
items.claim: King Harold Godwinson fought two major battles in 1066. What happened?

options.text: Hastings was his only battle of the year
He defeated Harald Hardrada and Tostig at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, then marched 250 miles south and lost to William at Hastings on 14 October
He won at Hastings but died of wounds soon after
He defeated William at Hastings, then was killed by Harald Hardrada

items.reveal:
Harald Hardrada of Norway and Harold's exiled brother Tostig landed in Yorkshire in September 1066. Harold marched north and crushed them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September — Hardrada and Tostig were killed.

Three days later William of Normandy landed at Pevensey. Harold's exhausted army marched south and met William at Senlac Hill near Hastings on 14 October. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Harold's death; the Bayeux Tapestry depicts a figure with an arrow to the eye, though the identification is debated.
items.why: The Conquest is taught as a single event. It was actually a year of crisis with two invasions, one of which Harold won. Without Stamford Bridge weakening his army, Hastings might have gone the other way.

items.title: The Hundred Years War lasted 116 years
items.claim: When did the Hundred Years War begin and end?

options.text: 1337 (Edward III claims the French throne) to 1453 (Battle of Castillon) — 116 years, with long truces in between

items.reveal_title: A name invented in the 19th century
items.reveal:
The phrase 'Hundred Years War' was coined by French historians in the 1860s. Contemporaries did not see it as a single conflict but as a series of campaigns separated by long peaces (e.g. the Treaty of Brétigny, 1360).

Major English victories: Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356), Agincourt (1415). Major French recoveries: Du Guesclin's reconquests under Charles V, and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429). It ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 — three months before Constantinople fell.
items.why: Periodisation is a historical choice, not a fact. A '100 years' war that was actually 116, mostly truce, and named four centuries later is a useful reminder.
